messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 64

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no bullet points.

Musa Adeyemi, a 55-year-old married African American man, had spent most of his adult life working around danger, and for years he had taken pride in being the person who could stay calm when everyone else was panicking. As a bomb disposal technician, he was used to controlled fear, to calculating distances, checking equipment, and trusting procedure. The event that changed him came not from his job but from a natural disaster during a deployment to assist after a major hurricane on the Gulf Coast. Musa and his team had been helping clear roads and inspect damaged buildings when a levee failed after days of relentless rain. He remembers the sound first, a deep cracking roar that seemed to come up through the ground, followed by the sight of water rushing through the streets with terrifying speed, carrying debris, cars, and pieces of houses. A child’s backpack floated past him, and then a wall of water struck the block where they were working. He was thrown against a truck, submerged briefly, and trapped in a tangle of broken fencing and branches while hearing people scream from nearby rooftops. One older man, who had been calling for help from a porch, disappeared when the structure gave way. Musa was pulled free by another responder, but from that moment he felt certain that he had failed to save someone who might have lived.

In the weeks after the hurricane, Musa expected the usual exhaustion and soreness to pass, but instead he began reliving the scene in fragments that arrived without warning. The roar of rushing water would come back to him vividly when he heard a storm drain gurgle outside his home, when a semi passed on the freeway, or when his wife ran the washing machine and the sound of water filling the drum suddenly made his chest tighten. He found himself waking in the night drenched in sweat, certain he could hear people shouting for help. He would sit up in the dark, his heart pounding, scanning the bedroom as if he needed to locate a threat. Sometimes he would see, just for a moment, the image of the man on the porch or the floating backpack, and he would feel a wave of guilt and shame, telling himself that a trained man should have done more, moved faster, known what to do. He began to believe that his competence had been an illusion and that if a disaster like that happened again, he would freeze or make a fatal mistake.

Musa’s world narrowed in ways that made sense to him at first. He stopped taking weekend drives with his wife near the river because even the sight of swollen water made his stomach turn. He avoided news coverage of hurricanes, skipped weather alerts when he could, and quietly asked his wife to turn off emergency broadcasts if they came on in the evening. At work, he became increasingly tense during training exercises that involved rescue scenarios or flood response. He found excuses to stay in the vehicle during rainstorms and delegated tasks he once handled confidently. He told himself this was prudence, not fear, because staying away from water and disaster reminders seemed like the only way to keep the images from flooding back into his mind. Yet the avoidance cost him. He became detached from colleagues and stopped joining his crew after shifts. At home, he was irritable and emotionally flat, reacting sharply to small noises or unexpected interruptions. His wife noticed that he startled when doors slammed, and that he sat with his back to the wall in restaurants, watching exits with a vigilance that never fully relaxed.

Over time, Musa’s sleep worsened, and with it his patience and concentration. He began checking weather apps repeatedly, sometimes dozens of times a day, not because it reassured him for long but because uncertainty felt unbearable. He would become angry at himself for being “soft,” then more frightened by the possibility that he was not soft at all but permanently altered. He started to think of the world as unpredictable and dangerous, and of himself as exposed in a way he had never been before. Even on clear days he felt on edge, as if another disaster could break through at any moment. He stopped attending church regularly because the crowd and the enclosed space made him feel trapped, and because after services he often had to walk past a drainage canal that could trigger the same surge of dread. His wife urged him to talk to someone, but he resisted, saying he had seen too much in his career to need counseling. Privately, he feared that if he opened the memories, they would become stronger and he would not be able to contain them.

By the time Musa sought help, he had been living with these symptoms for over a year. The immediate trigger was the forecast of another severe storm, which sent him into several nights of near-total insomnia and one episode in which he had to pull over while driving because a burst pipe beside the road made him feel as though the flood was happening again. He realized then that he was no longer simply managing a bad memory; he was organizing his entire life around avoiding it. What finally brought him in was his fear that his vigilance was starting to fail at work and that one day he would make a dangerous error because he was too distracted by what was happening inside his head. At the same time, he hoped that treatment might help him sleep, trust his own mind again, and stop feeling as though the water were always just behind him.
